vignette:
**Patient:** 33-year-old married male, South Eastern Asian, Physical Therapist
**PCL-5:** 38

---

Michael came to see me six weeks ago, referred by his primary care physician after his wife insisted something was "fundamentally wrong." He sits forward in the chair, hands clasped, posture that of a man used to fixing things. In his clinic, he is the one people trust with their bodies—he reassures them, guides them, celebrates their small victories. But when he talks about himself, his voice drops to something almost apologetic.

The accident happened fourteen months ago, on a Tuesday evening in late October. He was driving home from a continuing education seminar on manual therapy techniques. It was raining—not hard, but the kind of steady drizzle that makes the highway slick. He remembers the brake lights of the semi-truck ahead of him flaring red, remembers thinking *that's too fast, that's too sudden*, and then the world became noise and pressure and glass.

He was stopped in time. The car behind him was not. The impact shoved his sedan into the truck's trailer, then spun him across two lanes. When the car finally stopped, he was facing oncoming traffic. He remembers the smell of hot metal and the sound of his own breathing, ragged and too fast. The airbag had deployed, burning his forearms. His neck was in spasm. But he could move his fingers. He could move his toes.

What he cannot forget is the man in the car behind him. Michael got out, walked back on unsteady legs, and found him. The man was unconscious, bleeding from a cut on his scalp, his car crumpled to the driver's door. Michael—the physical therapist, the fixer—stood in the rain and did nothing. He had no tools. No equipment. No permission. He just stood there, holding the man's hand through the broken window, until the paramedics arrived. The man survived. Michael tells me this as if it's a failure.

Since that night, Michael has stopped driving on the highway. He takes surface streets to work, adding forty minutes to his commute each way. He tells his wife it's because he likes the scenery. He tells himself it's a reasonable accommodation. But last month, when a patient with a cervical strain described being rear-ended at a stoplight, Michael felt his chest tighten, his vision narrow. He excused himself to the bathroom and sat on the floor for ten minutes, counting his breaths.

He has nightmares. Not every night, but three or four times a week. They are not the accident itself. They are variations: he is in the car and the brakes do nothing; he is standing on the highway and no one sees him; he is holding the man's hand but the hand becomes a skeleton. He wakes gasping, soaked in sweat, and does not go back to sleep. He has learned to get up quietly, so his wife does not worry.

At work, he is competent but distant. He no longer jokes with patients during their exercises. He finds himself irritated by small things—a patient who cancels last minute, a colleague who leaves equipment out. He knows this is not like him. He was the one who stayed late, who remembered birthdays, who made the clinic feel warm. Now, he does his job. He goes home. He sits on the couch and scrolls his phone until it is time to sleep.

His wife told me he used to love cooking. Now, she does most of it. He eats because he should. He has lost twelve pounds.

When I asked him what he wants from therapy, he looked at the floor for a long time. Then he said, "I just want to stop feeling like I'm still in that car."
